name: leapfrog (LeapMap concurrent hash map)
verdict_reason: On a read-heavy mix LeapMap reached 148.0 Mops/s at 16 threads against 11.7 for RwLock<HashMap>, about 12.6x, close to the README's 'around 13.5x', and it led DashMap and flurry. Single-threaded it is slightly slower than the locked map.
tier_reason: Public benchmark fork with result CSVs, CPU, OS and LTO/codegen-units flags stated; first-party.
claimed_speedup: Claimed: around 13.5x faster than RwLock<HashMap> on 16 cores. Table: 148.0 vs 11.7 Mops/s at 16 threads on Ryzen 9 3950X (about 12.6x, derived from page data), 17.8 vs 19.4 at 1 thread; Apple M2 Max: 106.1 vs 3.4 at 12 threads.
workload: bustle read-heavy mix (98% reads, 1% insert, 1% remove) with u64 keys and FxHash.
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 3950X (16 cores); Apple M2 Max (12 cores)
platforms: All targets with std; needs nightly allocator_api or the stable_alloc feature
one_liner: Lock-free concurrent map using leapfrog probing; about 12x RwLock<HashMap> throughput at 16 threads on reads, with value-type restrictions.
how_it_is_fast: LeapMap is an open-addressing table where each bucket stores offsets to the next probe positions (leapfrog probing), so lookups jump directly along a key's probe chain. Keys and values that fit in atomics are read and written with atomic operations and no locks; other types fall back to fine-grained spinlocks.
use_it_when: Read-heavy shared maps with small, atomic-friendly key and value types such as integers.
skip_it_when: You cannot reserve two values of the value type: the Value trait needs a null and a redirect sentinel (MAX and MAX-1 for integers).
Single-threaded access, where RwLock<HashMap> was slightly faster.
You need a widely used, heavily reviewed crate: it has about 32 thousand downloads.
caveats: First-party numbers; the README's 13.5x is higher than its own table's 12.6x.
All maps in the table used FxHash; the baseline was parking_lot's RwLock, measured before std's RwLock moved to futexes on Linux in Rust 1.62.
tradeoffs: Reserved sentinel values in the value type.
Requires a nightly feature or the stable_alloc compatibility feature.

evidence.quote: Compared to `RwLock<HashMap>`, on 16 cores the `LeapMap` is around 13.5x faster.
A snapshot of the results for the LeapMap on a read heavy workload using a 16 core AMD 3950x CPU
